entities.summary:
Xenophanes of Colophon (c. 570 – c. 477 BCE) was a foundational pre-Socratic thinker, an itinerant poet-philosopher from Ionia who profoundly challenged traditional Greek polytheism and anthropomorphic deities. Operating across the Greek-speaking world from Magna Graecia to his native Asia Minor, his sharp critiques of Homer and Hesiod laid intellectual groundwork for subsequent philosophical inquiries into theology, epistemology, and cosmology, marking a pivotal shift from mythos to logos in the nascent Western intellectual tradition. His radical monotheistic or panentheistic leanings and emphasis on human fallibility in knowledge acquisition positioned him as a crucial precursor to Eleatic philosophy and later Skepticism.

Xenophanes's primary contributions are preserved through fragments of his elegiac and hexameter poems, which he recited during his extensive travels as a rhapsode. He famously declared that if 'oxen and horses and lions had hands... then horses would draw figures of gods like horses, and oxen like oxen,' directly mocking the anthropomorphic representations of Olympian gods. Furthermore, he posited a single, all-seeing, all-hearing, and all-thinking God, immobile and eternal, distinct from human form or passions, thereby introducing a concept of divine unity that contrasted sharply with the chaotic pantheon of Zeus, Hera, and Apollo. His cosmological theories, though rudimentary, included observations on fossils and geological change, suggesting an early empirical curiosity.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Xenophanes's radical critique of anthropomorphic deities and his proto-monotheistic views profoundly influenced the Eleatic school and subsequent philosophical theology, initiating a shift from mythological to rational inquiry about the divine. His epistemological skepticism also laid foundational groundwork for later Skepticism in Western thought.
